data.text:
'MAG-IINGAY SA EDSA': YOUTH, PROGRESSIVE GROUPS STAGE NOISE BARRAGE FOR ACCOUNTABILITY

Progressive groups staged a "White Friday Noise Barrage" at the historic People Power Monument to demand accountability in the multibillion-peso flood control scandal.

Led by Akbayan Partylist, Akbayan Youth, Youth Against Kurakot (YAK!), the Student Council Alliance of the Philippines (SCAP), and Tindig Pilipinas, the protest built on the momentum of the recent Trillion Peso March and amplified calls for transparency and punishment of corrupt politicians and contractors.

Akbayan Youth Secretary General and YAK! convenor Khylla Meneses said public outrage remains unresolved, describing the resignation of Ako Bicol Party-list Rep. Zaldy Co and Vice President Sara Duterte's budget request as a political spectacle aimed at dodging scrutiny.

SCAP Secretary General Matthew Silverio noted the growing unrest in schools and universities, pointing to student actions that reflect mounting frustration with corruption.

The groups pledged to sustain their campaign for transparency and reforms until full accountability is achieved.

📷 Akbayan Partylist

A typhoon blew into the northern #Philippines on Friday, complicating the country's disaster response to a deadly earthquake in a central province and two other recent storms.

#Typhoon Matmo blew into Dinapigue town in Isabela province from the Pacific with sustained winds up to 130 kph and was to blow northwestward over a vast agricultural valley and mountain provinces, where residents in some flood- and landslide-prone villages were evacuating.

quoted_tweet.text:
JPN media Yomiuri reports that Japan🇯🇵 and Taiwan🇹🇼 conducted a bilateral coast guard exercise off Japan's southeastern Sakishima Islands in June, with both sides seeking to make such training a regular practice: https://t.co/RjMo3GOqCm.

■ Translation: Japan and Taiwan Coast Guards to Regularise Joint Training
– Large Patrol Vessels Dispatched off the Sakishima Islands in June

It has come to light that the Japan Coast Guard (JCG) and Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA, the counterpart to the JCG) are working to make joint maritime training a regular occurrence. They are also considering exercises involving allied and like-minded countries. In June, both sides dispatched large patrol vessels off the Sakishima Islands in Okinawa Prefecture to conduct their second training exercise since Japan and Taiwan severed diplomatic ties, following the first one off Chiba Prefecture last year. This represents a step toward strengthening cooperation in waters close to the East and South China Seas and around Taiwan, where Chinese vessels have been intensifying coercive activities.

According to Taiwan-related sources, the participants included the helicopter-equipped patrol vessel Mizuho (134 meters in length, 6,000 gross tons) from the Nagoya Coast Guard Office, and the Yunlin (126 meters, 5,919 gross tons), one of the largest patrol vessels of the CGA.

In mid-June, the two vessels carried out joint training in international waters south of the Sakishima Islands, assuming a maritime rescue scenario. Unlike the July 2024 training off the Boso Peninsula in Chiba Prefecture, this exercise involved the ships approaching to within visible range of one another, thereby strengthening on-site cooperation through information sharing and coordination of search areas. After the exercise, Mizuho proceeded to Southeast Asia to conduct training with Malaysian maritime authorities and to engage in counter-piracy vigilance.

Since the severing of diplomatic relations in 1972, Japan and Taiwan have maintained working-level ties through the “Japan–Taiwan Exchange Association” on the Japanese side and the “Taiwan–Japan Relations Association” on the Taiwanese side. The Japanese government officially positions these training exercises as part of “exchanges” under memorandums of understanding on maritime rescue concluded between the two associations in 2017 and 2024.

However, in addition to these MOUs, the JCG and CGA have in recent years discreetly exchanged senior officials—including the CGA Director-General—sending them to Taipei and Tokyo for discussions, consultations, and site visits, thereby deepening cooperative ties. The backdrop is China’s increasingly coercive activities in the waters surrounding the Senkaku Islands in Okinawa and around Taiwan. In early September, ruling party lawmakers from Japan and Taiwan also met in Taipei to discuss cooperation between the two agencies and personnel exchanges.

Beyond cooperation with Taiwan, the JCG has been layering partnerships in the field of maritime security with a range of bilateral and “minilateral” frameworks, including: Japan–U.S., Japan–Philippines, Japan–India, Japan–U.S.–ROK, Japan–U.S.–Philippines, and Japan–U.S.–Australia–India, in order to advance the maintenance and strengthening of a maritime order based on the “rule of law.”
